actions.justification: Mandatory first step. Patient has tachycardia (HR 105) with hematemesis and melena; hemodynamic status assessment is critical to guide resuscitation in suspected upper GI bleed with cirrhosis.
Mandatory assessment. Full vital sign assessment is required to establish baseline and identify severity of hemodynamic compromise in this patient with active GI bleeding.
Mandatory. Large-bore IV access is essential for fluid resuscitation and medication administration in active upper GI hemorrhage.
Mandatory: CBC to assess hemoglobin/hematocrit and guide transfusion decisions in this patient with active GI bleeding.
Mandatory: Coagulation studies (PT/INR) are critical in a cirrhotic patient with GI bleeding due to likely coagulopathy.
Mandatory: Type and crossmatch required to prepare packed RBCs for potential transfusion in active GI hemorrhage.

Assess electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, and glucose in a cirrhotic patient with GI bleeding; BUN:creatinine ratio helps confirm upper GI source and renal function is critical before treatment decisions.

Patient has cirrhosis with hematemesis and melena — high suspicion for variceal bleeding. Octreotide (somatostatin analogue) reduces portal pressure and is first-line pharmacologic therapy for suspected variceal upper GI bleeding per AASLD/ACG guidelines, should be started early.
Urgent GI consultation needed for early endoscopy (within 12 hours per guidelines) in this cirrhotic patient with active upper GI bleeding for diagnosis and potential endoscopic hemostasis.

Lactate helps assess tissue perfusion and severity of hemorrhagic shock in this cirrhotic patient with hematemesis and tachycardia (HR 105). Elevated lactate would indicate inadequate perfusion despite relatively preserved BP.

Type and crossmatch is essential to prepare packed RBCs for potential transfusion. Given active upper GI bleeding with tachycardia, blood products may be needed urgently. CBC was ordered but crossmatch ensures blood is available.

Prokinetic agent (e.g., erythromycin or metoclopramide) given before endoscopy improves gastric visualization by promoting gastric emptying of blood and clots, increasing diagnostic and therapeutic yield of upcoming endoscopy in this cirrhotic patient with hematemesis.

Patient has tachycardia (HR 105) with hematemesis/melena and cirrhosis, suggesting volume depletion. IV crystalloid bolus indicated for hemodynamic resuscitation while awaiting blood products and pending labs.
IV PPI (proton pump inhibitor) is indicated in upper GI bleeding to reduce acid exposure and stabilize clots. Appropriate empiric therapy pending endoscopy.
Serial CBC monitoring is critical in active GI bleeding to track hemoglobin trend and guide transfusion decisions (transfuse if Hgb <7 in cirrhosis patients).

Serial CBC monitoring is essential in this patient with active GI bleeding (hematemesis/melena) and cirrhosis. Initial CBC is pending; a repeat order ensures trending of hemoglobin to guide transfusion decisions (threshold Hgb <7 for transfusion in UGIB with cirrhosis per guidelines).

This cirrhotic patient with hematemesis and melena, HR 105 suggesting hemodynamic compromise, should receive packed RBCs if Hgb <7 g/dL per UGIB/cirrhosis transfusion guidelines to stabilize hemoglobin while awaiting endoscopy.

Surgical consultation is prudent early in a cirrhotic patient with active upper GI bleeding in case endoscopic therapy fails and surgical or TIPS intervention becomes necessary. Early involvement improves response time.

Patient with cirrhosis, hematemesis, and tachycardia (HR 105) is at risk for tissue hypoperfusion. Trending lactate helps assess adequacy of resuscitation and severity of hemorrhagic shock, guiding further fluid and blood product management.

CT abdomen with contrast can help identify the source and extent of GI bleeding in this cirrhotic patient (e.g., varices, portal hypertension complications), especially if endoscopy findings are inconclusive or to assess for other abdominal pathology contributing to presentation.

Patient with cirrhosis presenting with hematemesis and melena (likely variceal or other GI bleed) remains hemodynamically tenuous (HR 105). With GI consulted, PPI/octreotide given, and labs pending, angiography can help identify and potentially treat the bleeding source if endoscopy is not immediately available or if the bleed is arterial in nature. This is the only available action remaining in the current phase.

Patient with cirrhosis and active GI bleed — assessing mental status is critical to detect hepatic encephalopathy, which is a common complication in cirrhotic patients with upper GI bleeding and affects management decisions.

Patient with cirrhosis presenting with hematemesis and melena requires urgent upper endoscopy (EGD) for diagnosis and treatment of suspected variceal or peptic ulcer bleeding. Octreotide and PPI have been initiated; endoscopy is the definitive next step per GI bleed guidelines.
Urine output monitoring is essential in this hemodynamically borderline patient (HR 105, MAP 73) with cirrhosis to assess end-organ perfusion and guide fluid resuscitation.
